title: Document stores with MongoDB
goal: By the end you can shape a payment as one MongoDB document and change it atomically, read what explain() says an index did, turn a SQL GROUP BY into an aggregation pipeline, and say which writes survive a primary failover under w:1 and w:"majority".

warmup.q: A three-member MongoDB 9.0 replica set. Your service inserts a payment with `{ w: 1 }` and gets `acknowledged: true`. A second later the primary is cut off from the network and another member is elected. What happens to that payment?
options: It's safe: acknowledged means it's on the primary's disk, and the new primary copies it from there
It can disappear: if no secondary had it yet, the old primary rolls it back when it rejoins, and the client is never told
MongoDB holds the election until every acknowledged write has reached a secondary
The client gets an error later, when the rollback happens
warmup.why: `w: 1` means only the primary had the write when the client heard OK. The new primary is elected by the members that can still talk to each other, and it doesn't have the write. When the old primary rejoins, it rolls back to the last point it shares with the new primary and saves the undone documents in a rollback directory. Nothing waits for the old primary's writes, and no error reaches the client. That's why the default since MongoDB 5.0 is `w: "majority"`.

sections.h: A document holds one payment and everything read with it
sections.body:
In Oracle, a payment with two refunds is three rows in two tables, and the payment screen joins them. MongoDB stores a document instead: one JSON-like tree with nested objects and arrays. On disk and on the wire it's BSON, binary JSON, which adds the types JSON lacks: 32- and 64-bit integers, `Decimal128`, a date (UTC milliseconds), `ObjectId` and binary data. Every document has an `_id`, its primary key, unique in its collection, and a document can be at most 16 MB.

Build the payment one version at a time. Version 1 copies the tables: a `payments` collection and a `refunds` collection, each refund holding its payment's id. The screen now makes two reads. Worse, the rule "refunds never add up to more than the payment" spans two documents, so checking and writing it safely needs a multi-document transaction (lesson 10).

Version 2 puts the refunds inside the payment, in an array, next to a running total, `refundedMinor`. One read returns everything the screen shows. And a write to one document is atomic in MongoDB: a single `updateOne` can check the rule and change the document, and no other write can slip in between. The refund in the Try-it is one update whose filter says "only if `refundedMinor` plus this refund is at most `amountMinor`", and whose update pushes the refund and adds to the total. Two refunds that race for the last 1,000 can't both win, because the second one's filter no longer matches. That's lesson 2's rule at work: embed what's read and changed together and stays bounded (a payment has a handful of refunds at most), reference what grows without limit.

Types matter more than they look. `mongosh` stores a small whole number as a 32-bit `int`, and a Kotlin `Long` sent through the Java driver becomes a 64-bit `long`. An amount that arrives as the string "42.50" from an old import job is stored as a string, and every sum then skips it.

That's where "NoSQL means no schema" goes wrong. A collection has no fixed columns, but you can attach a validator, a `$jsonSchema` that every write must pass, or MongoDB rejects it with error 121, "Document failed validation", and says which rule failed. The default level, `strict`, checks every insert and update, but not the documents already there. MongoDB 9.0 added a stricter level, `constraint`: to switch it on, MongoDB scans the whole collection and refuses if any document breaks the rules, and from then on it guarantees that every document passes. The Try-it trips over exactly that old string.

**In MongoDB the document is the unit of everything: a write is atomic for one document, an index entry points at one document, a pipeline passes documents from stage to stage, and a replica set copies document changes in the order one primary applied them.** Each section below takes one of those.

sections.h: An index is a sorted list of keys that point at documents
sections.body:
Lesson 2 built the index for AP3, `{ merchantId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 }`, and its `cost()` helper boiled `explain()` down to four numbers. Each number comes from one part of the plan, and reading plans is a daily skill.

An index is a sorted list of keys, each pointing at one document's record. `IXSCAN` walks a range of that list, and `keysExamined` counts the keys it touched. `FETCH` loads the document behind each key, and `docsExamined` counts those. `COLLSCAN` reads every document in the collection. `SORT` sorts in memory, because the order the query wants isn't an index order. A healthy query has keys examined, documents examined and documents returned close together, as lesson 2's 5, 5 and 5. When thousands of keys or documents are read to return five, the index doesn't match the query.

A query can skip the documents altogether. If it asks only for fields the index holds, and leaves out `_id`, MongoDB answers from the index alone. That's a covered query: the plan says `PROJECTION_COVERED` and `docsExamined` is 0. A screen that lists only times and amounts can be served that way.

Arrays get one index entry per element. An index on `refunds.refundId` is a multikey index: a payment with three refunds has three entries, each pointing at the same payment. "Which payment owns refund ref-1?" becomes a one-key lookup. Every write pays for every entry, so a payment with 20 refunds updates 20 entries in that index.

AP4, the idempotency key, needs a unique index, and it hides a trap. A document without the field is indexed as if the field were null, and a unique index allows only one null, so on a collection where most payments have no key the index can't even be built. Make it partial, indexing only documents where the field is a string, and a second use of the key fails with error E11000, "duplicate key".

Each index is another sorted list that every insert and update must maintain. Lesson 2's rule holds here too: add one for an access pattern you've written down, and check with `explain()` that the query uses it.

sections.h: The aggregation pipeline passes documents from stage to stage
sections.body:
Finance wants M-0042's day: how many payments per status, the total amount, the largest one. In SQL that's a `GROUP BY`. MongoDB's answer is the aggregation pipeline: an array of stages, where each stage takes documents in and passes documents on, in order.

The stages map onto SQL closely enough to translate by hand. `$match` is `WHERE`. `$group` is `GROUP BY`, with accumulators such as `$sum`, `$avg` and `$max` for the aggregates; its `_id` is the grouping key. `$sort` is `ORDER BY`, `$project` is the select list, and `$limit` is `FETCH FIRST`. `$unwind` turns one document with an array into one document per element, which is how you'd total refunds across payments. `$lookup` is a left outer join to another collection.

Order matters, because each stage only sees what the previous one passed on. Put `$match` first and the query planner can use an index for it, so only the matching documents enter the pipeline. The Try-it's plan shows it: `GROUP > FETCH > IXSCAN`, 202 keys and 200 documents for M-0042's 200 payments. The AP3 index serves the match on `merchantId`, then has to skip over the `status` field it doesn't care about, which costs the two extra keys. In MongoDB 9.0 the newer execution engine runs the `$group` inside that same plan.

`$group` and `$sort` are blocking: they have to see every input document before they can emit anything, so they hold state in memory. Each stage may use 100 MB before it must spill to disk, and MongoDB 9.0 adds a limit for a whole operation: 1 GB or 20% of the server's memory, whichever is bigger. A report over a year of payments should `$match` the smallest slice it can, as early as it can.

Take a position on `$lookup`. It's fine for a report that runs now and then. If a hot path joins on every read, the document has the wrong shape: embed the data, or copy the few fields the read needs, the way lesson 2 copied a summary of recent payments into the account.

sections.h: A replica set: one primary orders the writes, and a majority decides what survives
sections.body:
A single `mongod` runs on one machine, and when that machine dies, payments stop. So production MongoDB is a replica set: several members holding copies, normally three. One member, the primary, takes every write. It applies the write and records it in its oplog, a capped collection (`local.oplog.rs`) where each entry describes one change, usually to one document, in the order the primary applied them. The secondaries pull the oplog and replay it. That's the leader-based family from lesson 6: one copy puts writes in order, and nobody merges timestamps.

What if the primary dies? The members send each other heartbeats. If the secondaries hear nothing from the primary for `electionTimeoutMillis`, 10 seconds by default, one of them calls an election, and it needs votes from a majority of the voting members: 2 of 3. The MongoDB docs say an election should typically take no more than 12 seconds. A primary that can see only a minority steps down by itself. Two sides of a network cut can't both hold a majority, so there's never a second primary taking writes for long.

When may the client hear "OK"? That's the write concern. `w: 1` acknowledges once the primary has the write. `w: "majority"` waits until a majority of members have it in their oplogs, and it's been the default since MongoDB 5.0 for most deployments. In a healthy three-member set the difference is a few milliseconds (lesson 9 measures it).

The difference shows during a failover, and the stepper walks through it. A member votes only for a candidate whose oplog is at least as recent as its own, so a write a majority holds is on any new primary. A write that only the old primary had isn't. When the old primary rejoins, it finds the last entry its oplog shares with the new primary and rolls back everything after it, saving the undone documents as BSON files under `<dbpath>/rollback/<collection uuid>/`. The client got its OK long ago, and nobody tells it.

Reads have a dial too, the read concern. `local`, the default, returns whatever the member has, including writes that may still be rolled back. `majority` returns only what a majority has. `linearizable` runs on the primary and returns every majority-acknowledged write that completed before the read began. For payments, leave writes at `w: "majority"`, treat a `wtimeout` error as "unknown" (the write isn't undone), and read from the primary, or with `majority` where a rolled-back read would hurt.

try.title: Lose an acknowledged write in a failover
steps: Make sure `env/mongo.yml` is down. From the `labs` folder, start a three-member replica set (about 30 seconds, about 1.5 GB of Docker memory). `env/mongo-rs.yml` starts the members, initiates `rs0` from mongo1's healthcheck and reports healthy once mongo1 is primary.
Run the commands below in order. Step 2 has to run within about 10 seconds of the `disconnect`, before mongo1 notices it's alone. Predict which of the four payments are left at the end.
The last command stops the set and deletes its data.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.src:
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml up -d --wait

# 1. a payment that every member gets: w:"majority"
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval 'db.payments.insertOne({_id: "pay-81701", amountMinor: 18000}, {writeConcern: {w: "majority"}})'

# 2. cut mongo1 off, then at once write to it: one w:1 write, one w:"majority" write
docker network disconnect sfz-mongo-rs_default sfz-mongo-rs-mongo1-1
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval 'db.payments.insertOne({_id: "pay-81723", amountMinor: 2500}, {writeConcern: {w: 1}})'
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval 'db.payments.insertOne({_id: "pay-81724", amountMinor: 1200}, {writeConcern: {w: "majority", wtimeout: 5000}})'

# 3. wait for the election, look from both sides, write to the new primary
sleep 15
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo2 mongosh --quiet --eval 'rs.status().members.map(m => m.name + " " + m.stateStr).join("\n")'
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh --quiet --eval 'const h = db.hello(); ({isWritablePrimary: h.isWritablePrimary, primary: h.primary})'
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo2 mongosh "mongodb://mongo2:27017,mongo3:27017/sfz?replicaSet=rs0" --quiet --eval 'db.payments.insertOne({_id: "pay-81730", amountMinor: 4250}, {writeConcern: {w: "majority"}})'

# 4. heal the cut, give mongo1 time to rejoin, then see what is left
docker network connect --alias mongo1 sfz-mongo-rs_default sfz-mongo-rs-mongo1-1
sleep 25
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh --quiet --eval 'rs.status().members.map(m => m.name + " " + m.stateStr).join("\n")'
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh "mongodb://mongo1:27017,mongo2:27017,mongo3:27017/sfz?replicaSet=rs0" --quiet --eval 'db.payments.find().toArray()'
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 bash -c 'ls -R /data/db/rollback; bsondump --quiet /data/db/rollback/*-*/removed.*.bson'

docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml down -v

refs.title: MongoDB: rollbacks during replica set failover
MongoDB: write concern (w, wtimeout, the majority default)

analogy: Think of a bank branch with one head teller and two assistants. Every transaction goes to the head teller, who writes it in the day book in order; the assistants copy the day book line by line. Telling a customer "done" as soon as the head teller has written the line is `w: 1`. Waiting until at least one assistant has copied it too is `w: "majority"`. If the head teller is locked in the back office, the two assistants agree that one of them takes over, because two of three is a majority. When the head teller comes out, any lines only they wrote get torn out and filed in an envelope, since the branch now follows the new day book. The analogy breaks on the envelope: in MongoDB nobody reads it unless an operator goes looking, and the customer who was told "done" is never called back.
in_your_world: Your Oracle primary with a Data Guard standby in maximum availability mode is the same idea as `w: "majority"`: commit waits for the standby, so a failover loses nothing. A Quarkus service using the MongoDB Java driver gets `w: "majority"` by default; the danger is someone setting `w: 1` "for speed" on the payments collection. Embed refunds and the status history in the payment document and use guarded single-document updates, and you need no transaction for the refund rule. When a write fails with a write concern timeout, treat it like a timeout from the card issuer: the write may have happened. A Temporal activity that retries it should use the payment id as `_id` or check an idempotency key with a partial unique index, so the retry can't create a second payment.
mistake: The most common mistake is treating `acknowledged: true` as "durable", and lowering the write concern to `w: 1` for throughput. In a healthy set nothing looks wrong, and the latency gain is real but small, a few milliseconds. Then a primary is cut off for a few seconds, takes writes no one else sees, and rolls them back when it rejoins. Payments the service confirmed vanish, with no error anywhere, and the only trace is a BSON file in a rollback directory. The fix: keep `w: "majority"` (the default since 5.0) for anything that matters, treat a write concern timeout as unknown rather than failed, and read with `majority` where acting on a rolled-back write would hurt.

compare.title: A merchant's daily totals: SQL and the aggregation pipeline

a.label: SQL (PostgreSQL or Oracle)
a.src:
SELECT status,
       COUNT(*)          AS payments,
       SUM(amount_minor) AS amount_minor,
       MAX(amount_minor) AS largest
FROM payment
WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042'
  AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-11-07 00:00:00'
  AND created_at <  TIMESTAMP '2026-11-08 00:00:00'
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status;

b.label: MongoDB aggregation
b.src:
db.payments.aggregate([
  { $match: { merchantId: "M-0042",                       // WHERE
              createdAt: { $gte: ISODate("2026-11-07T00:00:00Z"),
                           $lt:  ISODate("2026-11-08T00:00:00Z") } } },
  { $group: { _id: "$status",                              // GROUP BY
              payments:    { $sum: 1 },                     // COUNT(*)
              amountMinor: { $sum: "$amountMinor" },        // SUM
              largest:     { $max: "$amountMinor" } } },    // MAX
  { $sort: { _id: 1 } }                                    // ORDER BY
])

compare.note: The two say the same thing, and both planners use an index for the WHERE part. The difference is the order. SQL is declarative: the optimizer decides when to filter, group and sort. A pipeline runs its stages in the order you write them, with a few rewrites by the server, so `$match` belongs first or the index can't help. And a pipeline passes documents, not rows: `$group` can build arrays (`$push`) and nested results that SQL would need a second query or JSON functions for.

worked.title: Shape the payment document and its indexes from the access patterns

steps.say: Start from lesson 2's access patterns and mark which document answers each one. AP1 stays on the account document, with its capped summary of recent payments.
steps.code:
AP1  account's recent payments    accounts doc, recentPayments ($push + $slice)
AP2  payment by id                payments._id
AP3  merchant + status, newest     index { merchantId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 }
AP4  idempotency key used once     unique partial index on idempotencyKey
AP6  refunds of a payment          embedded in the payment (bounded)

steps.say: Write one payment the way it will be stored. Amounts are 64-bit integers in minor units, times are dates, refunds are inside, with the running total next to them.
steps.code:
{
  _id: "pay-81723", accountId: "A-1001", merchantId: "M-0042",
  status: "SETTLED", amountMinor: NumberLong(4250), currency: "EUR",
  createdAt: ISODate("2026-11-07T09:00:00Z"), idempotencyKey: "idem-7f3a",
  refundedMinor: NumberLong(1250),
  refunds: [ { refundId: "ref-1", amountMinor: NumberLong(1250), at: ISODate("2026-11-07T10:02:00Z") } ]
}

steps.say: Make the shape a rule. The validator fixes the types and bounds the array, which is what made embedding safe. On 9.0, upgrade an existing collection to `constraint` once it's clean.
steps.code:
db.createCollection("payments", { validator: { $jsonSchema: {
  bsonType: "object",
  required: ["accountId", "merchantId", "status", "amountMinor", "createdAt", "refundedMinor", "refunds"],
  properties: {
    status:        { enum: ["AUTHORIZED", "SETTLED", "FAILED"] },
    amountMinor:   { bsonType: "long", minimum: 1 },
    refundedMinor: { bsonType: "long", minimum: 0 },
    refunds:       { bsonType: "array", maxItems: 20 } } } } })

steps.say: Create one index per pattern that isn't `_id`, and nothing else. Each one is a sorted list every write has to maintain.
steps.code:
db.payments.createIndex({ merchantId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 })   // AP3
db.payments.createIndex({ idempotencyKey: 1 },                           // AP4
  { unique: true, partialFilterExpression: { idempotencyKey: { $type: "string" } } })
db.payments.createIndex({ "refunds.refundId": 1 })                     // support: refund -> payment

steps.say: Check each pattern with `explain()` before you ship. You want an `IXSCAN`, no `SORT`, and keys examined close to documents returned.
steps.code:
cost(db.payments.find({ merchantId: "M-0042", status: "FAILED" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(5))
// { plan: 'LIMIT > FETCH > IXSCAN', returned: 5, keysExamined: 5, docsExamined: 5 }

lab.title: Store payments as documents: embed, guard, index, aggregate
steps: Make sure Docker is running, then run the tests from the `labs` folder. The first run starts one `mongo:9.0` container through Testcontainers (a few seconds, plus the pull if you've never run `env/mongo.yml`). All nine tests fail.
Read `PaymentDocs.kt`. The schema and `createCollection` are given; every test writes into a collection with that validator, in a database of its own.
Write `toDocument` first: every other test seeds its data with it. The first two tests check the stored BSON types and that the validator accepts your documents and rejects bad ones.
Write `addRefund` as one `updateOne` with a guarded filter. The race test fires twenty refunds at once at a 10,000 payment and expects exactly ten to win.

Write `createIndexes`, `recentByMerchantStatus` and `dailyTotalsPipeline`. The tests run `explain()` on your query and your pipeline and check for an `IXSCAN`, no `SORT`, and 5 keys and 5 documents for 5 results. Swap `status` and `createdAt` in your index and watch the AP3 test fail.
hints: `Document("_id", p.paymentId).append(...)`. A Kotlin `Long` becomes BSON `long`; `Date.from(instant)` becomes a BSON date. The refunds are `p.refunds.map(::refundDocument)`.

The guard compares two fields of the same document, so it needs `Filters.expr`: `Document("\$lte", listOf(Document("\$add", listOf("\$refundedMinor", refund.amountMinor)), "\$amountMinor"))`. Return `modifiedCount == 1L`.

The pipeline is `listOf(Aggregates.match(...), Aggregates.group("\$status", Accumulators.sum("count", 1), ...), Aggregates.sort(Sorts.ascending("_id")))`. The day runs from `day.atStartOfDay(ZoneOffset.UTC)` to the next day's start, end excluded.

drill.title: The guarded refund and the write concerns, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the mongosh `updateOne` that adds a 1,250 refund `ref-2` to payment pay-81723 only if the payment is SETTLED and the refunds stay within the amount. Then write one line each: what `w: 1` and `w: "majority"` promise when the client hears OK, and what happens to each if the primary is cut off right after.

recap: A MongoDB document is a BSON tree with typed fields, an `_id` and a 16 MB limit. A write to one document is atomic, so embed what's read and changed together and bounded, like a payment's refunds, and guard the change in the update's filter.
Validators give collections a schema: `strict` checks every write, and 9.0's `constraint` level also checks every existing document before it switches on. Failed writes get error 121.

`explain()` tells you what a query read: `IXSCAN` keys, `FETCH`ed documents, `COLLSCAN`, in-memory `SORT`. Covered queries read no documents, array fields make multikey indexes, and a unique index on an optional field must be partial.
An aggregation pipeline passes documents through stages: `$match`, `$group`, `$sort`, `$project`, `$unwind`, `$lookup`. Put `$match` first so an index can serve it.

A replica set has one primary that orders writes in its oplog. Elections need a majority, after about 10 seconds of silence. `w: "majority"` (the default since 5.0) survives failover; a `w: 1` write can be rolled back into a file, with no error to the client.

quiz.q: Two support agents refund the last 1,000 of a payment at the same moment, each with the guarded `updateOne` from this lesson. What happens?
options: Both refunds apply, because MongoDB has no transactions here
MongoDB raises a write conflict and both fail
The second update waits for a lock, then applies, refunding 2,000
One applies; the other's filter no longer matches, so it modifies nothing
quiz.why: MongoDB checks the filter and applies the update to one document atomically. After the first refund, `refundedMinor + 1000 <= amountMinor` is false, so the second update matches nothing and returns `modifiedCount: 0`. Two separate statements, a read then a write, would race; one guarded update can't. The lab's race test fires twenty at once.

quiz.q: `explain("executionStats")` on a query that returns 5 payments shows `keysExamined: 4800, docsExamined: 4800`. What does that tell you?
options: The query is fine: it used an index, so it's fast
An index was used, but it doesn't match the query: MongoDB walked 4,800 keys and loaded 4,800 documents to keep 5
The collection is fragmented and needs compacting
MongoDB counted the documents twice because of the projection
quiz.why: Keys examined, documents examined and documents returned should be close. Here an index served part of the filter, maybe just `merchantId`, and everything else was checked document by document. Reorder or extend the index to equality, sort, range (lesson 2) until the numbers meet.

quiz.q: `db.payments.createIndex({ idempotencyKey: 1 }, { unique: true })` fails with E11000 on `{ idempotencyKey: null }`. Only 3 payments have a key. Why?
options: Every payment without the field is indexed as null, and a unique index allows one null
Unique indexes can't be built on a collection that already has documents
Two of the three keys are duplicates
The field name is reserved
quiz.why: A missing field is indexed as null, so 997 payments all have the same key, null. A `partialFilterExpression` such as `{ idempotencyKey: { $type: "string" } }` indexes only payments that have a key, and uniqueness then applies just to them. Nothing in the error says the three real keys collide.

quiz.q: A replica set's primary is cut off for 20 seconds. Before it notices, it acknowledges one `w: 1` insert, and one `w: "majority", wtimeout: 5000` insert fails with a write concern timeout. After it rejoins, what's left of the two?
options: Both survive: the old primary sends them to the new primary when it rejoins
The `w: 1` insert survives; the failed one is gone
Neither is in the collection; both are in the old primary's rollback files
Only the failed one survives, because it asked for a majority
quiz.why: Neither reached a second member, so neither is on the new primary, and the rejoining member rolls back everything after the last point it shares with it. The Try-it found pay-81723 and pay-81724 side by side in the rollback file. The `w: 1` client was told OK and the other was told "error"; both were wrong about what would happen.

quiz.q: From lesson 6: Cassandra and a MongoDB replica set both keep three copies. What's different about how they order writes to the same payment?
options: Nothing: both send every write to all copies and keep the highest timestamp
Both elect a leader per key with Paxos
MongoDB is leaderless; Cassandra has a primary per partition
MongoDB's primary applies writes in one order and secondaries replay its oplog; Cassandra's coordinators send writes to all replicas and the highest timestamp wins
quiz.why: MongoDB is the leader-based family: one primary decides the order, so two concurrent updates to one document are applied one after the other. Cassandra is leaderless, as in Dynamo: any node coordinates, replicas reconcile by timestamp, and a concurrent write can silently lose. `w: "majority"` plays the role of W = 2 of 3, on top of a single order.

flashcards.front: What is a MongoDB write atomic over?
flashcards.back: One document. A single update can check a condition in its filter and change several fields and arrays of that document with no other write in between.

flashcards.front: What does `constraint` (MongoDB 9.0) add over the `strict` validation level?
flashcards.back: It scans every existing document when you switch it on, refuses if any break the rules, and then guarantees every document in the collection passes.
Walk index keys; load the documents they point at; read every document; sort in memory because no index gives the order.

flashcards.front: Why must a unique index on an optional field be partial?
flashcards.back: Documents without the field are indexed as null, and a unique index allows only one null.

flashcards.front: How long before a replica set elects a new primary?
flashcards.back: `electionTimeoutMillis` is 10 s by default; the docs say an election should typically finish within 12 s.
`w: 1`: the primary has it, and it can be rolled back if the primary fails over. `w: "majority"` (default since 5.0): a majority has it, and it survives failover.

flashcards.front: Where does a rolled-back write go?
flashcards.back: To BSON files under `<dbpath>/rollback/<collection uuid>/removed.<time>.bson` on the old primary. Read them with `bsondump`. Clients aren't told.

terms.plain: Binary JSON: MongoDB's storage and wire format, with types JSON lacks, such as 64-bit integers, dates and ObjectId.
Storing related data inside the parent document, such as a payment's refunds in an array, so one read and one atomic write cover both.
A `$jsonSchema` rule on a collection that every write must pass; levels strict, moderate and, in 9.0, constraint.
An index on an array field, with one entry per array element, each pointing at the document.
A list of stages ($match, $group, $sort, ...) that documents flow through in order; MongoDB's GROUP BY and more.
The primary's ordered log of document changes (`local.oplog.rs`) that secondaries copy and replay.
How many replica set members must have a write before the client hears OK: `w: 1` or `w: "majority"`.
A rejoining former primary undoing the writes the new primary never got, saving them to files.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate wants to set `w: 1` on the payments collection because "we measured 3 ms faster writes, and acknowledged is acknowledged". Explain what `w: 1` and `w: "majority"` each promise, and what happens to a `w: 1` payment in a failover.
explain_back.answer: With `w: 1` the client hears OK as soon as the primary has the write in its oplog. With `w: "majority"` it waits until two of our three members have it, which in a healthy set costs a few milliseconds. The difference only shows in a failover. If the primary is cut off, the other two elect a new primary after about 10 seconds, and a member only votes for a candidate whose oplog is at least as recent as its own, so every majority-acknowledged write is on the new primary. A `w: 1` write that hadn't reached a secondary isn't. When the old primary rejoins, it finds the last oplog entry it shares with the new primary and rolls back everything after it into a BSON file in its rollback directory. The payment we confirmed is simply gone from the collection, and no client gets an error. Three milliseconds isn't worth that for payments. Keep the default `w: "majority"`, and treat a write concern timeout as unknown, because the write isn't undone either.

deeper.body:
Read concern and write concern combine. MongoDB's causally consistent sessions promise read-your-writes and monotonic reads across members, but the defaults page is precise about when: only if the session's reads use `majority` read concern and its writes use `majority` write concern. With the defaults, reads use `local`, which "can return data that may be rolled back". Lesson 9 names these guarantees and shows where each one breaks.

Jepsen's 2020 analysis of MongoDB 4.2.6 is the cautionary tale. Transactions ignored the database and collection defaults and fell back to `local` reads and `w: 1` writes unless the transaction set its own concerns, and Jepsen lost acknowledged writes under network partitions. Read skew and other anomalies showed up even at the strongest settings, which MongoDB traced to a retry bug with a fix scheduled for 4.2.8. The recommendation still stands for every version: set read and write concern explicitly on each transaction, `snapshot` and `majority`.

In 2012 Abadi's PACELC paper classed MongoDB as PA/EC, partly because of its asynchronous replication and its "rollback directory". The default became `w: "majority"` in 5.0, so the class describes a configuration of its time, not the product. Lesson 9 uses PACELC properly.

The oplog is a capped collection: when it's full, the oldest entries go. A secondary that falls further behind than the oldest entry can't catch up by replaying and needs a full initial sync. Size the oplog for your longest expected outage, maintenance window included.

Arbiters are members that vote but hold no data. With two data members and one arbiter, a majority of data-bearing members is impossible during a failure, so MongoDB's implicit default write concern drops to `w: 1` for such sets. That's one more reason to run three data-bearing members.
